title: Dynamic programming laboratory
summary: Policy improvement, policy iteration and value iteration with every intermediate value function and policy shown. Step through evaluation and improvement one at a time, or value iteration sweep by sweep, and see which states change action. Fixtures from the draft: the 4×4 gridworld of Example 4.1 and the gambler's problem of Example 4.3.
guide: Run policy iteration on the gridworld from the equiprobable random policy: one improvement already gives an optimal policy, and the second evaluation confirms it (p. 98).
Run value iteration on the gridworld and watch $v_k$ become $-1, -2, -3$ (the number of steps to a corner) in a few sweeps.
Load the gambler's problem with $p_h = 0.4$. After value iteration, $v(50) = 0.4$, $v(25) = 0.16$ and $v(75) = 0.64$: staking boldly is optimal when the coin is unfavourable.

In the gambler's problem a stake of 0 is in the draft's action set and, with $\gamma = 1$, always ties for the maximum (it just keeps the capital). The lab therefore shows the smallest positive maximizing stake; the draft notes that the optimal policy is not unique.
Change $p_h$ to 0.55 and see how the optimal stakes change.

flags.note: Figure 4.3's policy iteration may never stop when equally good policies alternate (its caption says so).
flags.suggestion: The lab keeps an action while it is still among the maximizers, so it always stops.
